results.title: AWS Capacity Blocks GPU Rates Rise 20%
highlights:
AWS still posts July 1 Capacity Block GPU rates, Trainium stayed off the hike, and CoreWeave raised SKUs about 25 percent the same month.

Published

4 months ago

on

June 30, 2026

By

Harry

Amazon Web Services still posts the July 1 Capacity Block rates, and the next scheduled update is October 2026. The about 20% rise hit reserved Nvidia GPU time used to train and fine-tune models, not on-demand instances, and it left Trainium off the list.

Other clouds did not open a cheap overflow lane. CoreWeave raised SKUs about 25% in the same month and said near-term capacity was sold out.

## AWS Raised the Price of a Guaranteed Training Window

Capacity Blocks for ML are a booking product. A team pays up front for a future cluster in an EC2 UltraCluster, for a set number of days, so a training run does not die halfway through for lack of GPUs.

AWS says those reservation prices move with supply and demand. The public card is a published base rate, refreshed on a calendar, and a purchase locks the rate even if the block starts after the next refresh. On-demand list prices and other EC2 options were not part of the July notice, which closed with the line that all other prices remain unchanged.

That split is the whole move. Teams that can gamble on spare capacity keep the old menu. Teams that need a date certain for an H100, H200, or Blackwell cluster pay the new premium for the calendar slot.

Cloud economist Corey Quinn, who runs Last Week in AWS, rejected the supply-and-demand framing after the January rise, saying AWS was updating published base rates on the pricing page and that it was a policy decision, not supply and demand. July repeated the same shape: named families, a single effective date, a flat new per-chip rate across listed regions.

 

EC2 Capacity Blocks P6-B300 H100 hourly prices

## What AWS Capacity Blocks Cost After July 1

The current Capacity Blocks reservation rates match the July 1 notice, and AWS says those prices are scheduled to be updated next in October 2026. A block bought before that refresh keeps the rate paid at purchase.

JULY 1 CAPACITY BLOCK RATES

| Instance | Accelerators | US rate per chip | US rate per instance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| p6-b300.48xlarge | 8 x B300 | $14.04 | $112.32 |
| p6-b200.48xlarge | 8 x B200 | $12.355 | $98.84 |
| p5en.48xlarge | 8 x H200 | $6.865 | $54.92 |
| p5e.48xlarge | 8 x H200 | $5.97 | $47.76 |
| p5.48xlarge | 8 x H100 | $5.191 | $41.528 |

P6-B300 in AWS GovCloud (US-East) lists $14.625 per chip and $117.00 per instance. P5 outside the United States lists $4.720 per H100 and $37.76 per p5.48xlarge. P5en outside the United States lists $6.241 per chip and $49.928 per instance. P5e is $5.97 per H200 in every listed region. P4de, the A100 80GB line, is $2.214 per accelerator in available US regions.

P6-B300 instances pack eight Nvidia Blackwell Ultra GPUs with 2.1 TB of high-bandwidth GPU memory. AWS opened them in US East (N. Virginia) on May 6, 2026, after US West (Oregon) and GovCloud (US-East).

## 15 Percent in January Already Reset the Floor

July was the second Capacity Block rise of 2026. On Saturday, January 4, AWS lifted the same product about 15% without a separate customer email, after a pricing-page note that rates would be updated in January with no direction attached.

THE 2026 CAPACITY BLOCK RATE CARD

1. 2024 and 2025: AWS cut Capacity Block pricing three times, once in 2024 and twice in 2025, while a June 2025 promotion cut some On-Demand and Savings Plans GPU prices by up to 45%.
2. January 4, 2026: p5e.48xlarge moves from $34.61 to $39.80 per hour in most regions, and p5en.48xlarge moves from $36.18 to $41.61. An AWS spokesperson said the adjustment reflected supply and demand patterns expected that quarter.
3. July 1, 2026: New per-accelerator rates take effect for P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de. The H200 p5e.48xlarge instance rate goes from $39.80 to $47.76, a 20% step, and 38% above the $34.61 print from before January.
4. October 2026: AWS schedules the next update of the published reservation card. A block bought at the July rates keeps those rates even if it starts after the refresh.

The 38% stack is the p5e.48xlarge path, not a claim about every family. US P5en went from $41.61 after January to $54.92, which is a steeper step than 20%, so the honest read is the published chip rates, not a single percentage on every SKU.

...

The July notice named P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de, then said all other prices remain unchanged. Trn1 and Trn2 Capacity Blocks are still on the same public card as those Nvidia rows, at the prior reservation rates.

A trn1.32xlarge lists $9.532 per hour in US East (N. Virginia), Ohio, and Oregon, which is $0.596 per Trainium chip across 16 chips. A trn2.48xlarge in US East (Ohio) lists $35.7608 per hour, or $2.235 per Trainium2 chip across 16 chips. Those figures sit on the same page as the $14.04 B300 rate and were not in the July list.

...

You can inspect a price before you buy, and a search across dates returns the lowest-priced offering in range. Payment posts within 5 minutes to 12 hours. If it cannot be processed, the reservation moves to payment-failed and the block is released. Instances launched into a block must target the reservation ID and do not count against On-Demand instance limits.

...

### Did AWS Raise On-Demand GPU Instance Prices on July 1, 2026?

No. The July notice applied to Capacity Blocks for the named families and said all other prices remain unchanged, so On-Demand and Savings Plans GPU list prices were not part of that card. In June 2025 AWS had publicized cuts of up to 45% on some On-Demand and Savings Plans GPU instances, a promotion that did not cover Capacity Blocks.

...

### Were AWS Trainium Capacity Blocks Included in the July 2026 Price Rise?

No. The official notice listed P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de only. P6e-GB200 UltraServers in the US East (Dallas) Local Zone still list $10.582 per accelerator on the same pricing page and were not in that named set, which is how Trainium and that UltraServer line stayed on the prior reservation card.

results.title: AWS just broke its 20-year promise on cloud pricing | Prince Singh
highlights:
AWS just broke its 20-year promise on cloud pricing
For two decades, the assumption in cloud computing was simple: AWS prices only go down. That changed in January 2026.
→ AWS raised EC2 Capacity Block prices for ML/GPU workloads by ~15% across all regions — uniformly, on every region, with no advance notice beyond a vague "prices update in January" note on the pricing page.
→ The p5e.48xlarge instance (8x NVIDIA H200 GPUs) jumped from $34.61/hr to $39.80/hr. The p5en.48xlarge climbed from $36.18/hr to $41.61/hr. US West (N. California) saw even steeper hikes.
→ Effective July 1, 2026, AWS updated Capacity Block rates again — this time introducing pricing for new P6-B300 and P6-B200 (Blackwell-class) instances at $14.04 and $12.36 per accelerator-hour respectively.
→ The catch for enterprise customers: even those with negotiated Enterprise Discount Programs aren't shielded, since those discounts are typically percentage-based off the public list price — a 15% hike still flows straight to the bill.
→ Ironically, this came just months after AWS advertised "up to 45% price reductions" on GPU On-Demand and Savings Plans — though that announcement conveniently excluded Capacity Blocks.
What's NOT changing: AWS says On-Demand and Savings Plans pricing commitments remain intact. But Capacity Blocks are often the only practical way to actually secure high-demand GPU instances like H200s and Blackwells — so the "stable" on-demand price is somewhat theoretical for teams that actually need guaranteed capacity.
The bigger signal here isn't the dollar amount — it's the precedent. GPU compute has decoupled from the deflationary trend that defined cloud pricing for 20 years. Chip scarcity, surging AI demand, and dollar weakness are now bigger forces than Moore's Law efficiency gains.
If your AI infrastructure budget assumes flat or falling GPU costs over the next few years, this is the moment to stress-test that assumption.
#AWS #CloudComputing #FinOps #AI #CloudCosts #DevOps

results.title: GPU Compute Tightness Index — Web Pulse
highlights:
The GPU Compute Tightness Index fell to 43.8/100 as of June 29, 2026, entering Loose territory after a monthly drop of 13.7 points, indicating abundant idle AI infrastructure and supply exceeding near-term demand. Per-GPU readings show H100 at 37, B200 at 47, and H200 at 57, with spot discounts of 55%, 47%, and 31% below on-demand pricing.

...

The Compute Tightness Index sank to 43.8/100 as of 2026-06-29, pushing the blended gauge into Loose territory after a -13.7 pts monthly drop that pulled it under the prior 44–64 range. Per-GPU readings of 37 for H100, 47 for B200, and 57 for H200 correspond to spot discounts of 55%, 47%, and 31% below on-demand, signaling abundant idle AI infrastructure and supply that currently exceeds near-term training and inference demand. It is the input-side companion to the Token Demand Index (the output — tokens consumed).

← looser · 45 balanced · 60 tight · tighter →

As of 2026-06-29 the blended index sits at 43.8 (Loose) and has been loosening over the past 30 days (-13.7 pts). Listing-weighted across H100, H200 and B200 by on-demand market depth.

| GPU | On-demand $/hr | Spot $/hr | Spot discount | Listings | CTI | 30d |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B200 | $6.42 | $3.43 | 47% | 46 | 46.6 | ▼ -5.9 |
| H200 | $4.13 | $2.84 | 31% | 69 | 56.9 | ▼ -20.9 |
| H100 | $3.62 | $1.64 | 55% | 145 | 36.8 | ▼ -13.5 |
| MI355Xthin · excl. from blend | $8.60 | $0.00 | 100% | 2 | — | |

Spot discount = how far below on-demand the spot rate trades. A shrinking discount (rising CTI) means spare capacity is drying up; a widening discount (falling CTI) means idle GPUs are being dumped on spot. MI355X is tracked for coverage but excluded from the blended index — its listing count is too thin to weight reliably.

For each GPU on each day: `CTI = 100 × ( 0.8 · spot_avg/on_demand_avg + 0.2 · unavailable/(unavailable + on_demand_listings) )` . The scarcity term is the share of listed capacity that has gone dark (clamped to 1). The blended index is the listing-weighted mean across B200, H200 and H100 (weighted by on-demand listing count, a proxy for market depth). Inputs are the daily GetDeploying aggregate of public GPU rental listings — on-demand, reserved and spot averages plus availability — one snapshot per day.

results.title: AWS Raises EC2 Capacity Block Prices Amid GPU Shortage | TMC Insight
highlights:
### Key Takeaways

- AWS will raise EC2 Capacity Block pricing by about 20% starting July 1, marking its second increase of 2026.
- Enterprises face rising compute costs as hyperscalers compete for scarce Nvidia GPUs and high-bandwidth memory.
- Industry analysts expect AI infrastructure demand to keep accelerating, tightening supply further.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) is preparing another price hike for its EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML. The service, which lets customers reserve GPU instances across Nvidia hardware and AWS custom silicon up to eight weeks in advance, saw roughly a 15% increase in January. AWS is adding another increase of about 20% beginning July 1.

For example, an H200-based p5e.48xlarge instance cost around $34.61 per hour before January. After the July 1 adjustment, the same instance will run about $39 in most global regions, and $49.74 in the U.S. West. AWS stated that prices are updated periodically based on supply and demand.

...

Even with cloud spending rising quickly, the availability of GPUs continues to lag. Major cloud rivals including AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud are competing for scarce Nvidia H100 and H200 processors, as well as upcoming B100 GPUs. High-bandwidth memory and advanced accelerators remain constrained by tight DRAM production cycles and limited HBM supply. Long lead times and higher reservation costs make it harder for enterprises to secure required compute capacity.

results.title: Kidz AI Pivots from EdTech to Neocloud with $500M GPU Fund | HostDir
highlights:
# From EdTech to AI Cloud: Classover Rebrands as Kidz AI, Secures $500M for GPU Infrastructure

Classover, an AI education startup, rebrands as Kidz AI and raises $500.6 million to build GPU cloud infrastructure and data center capacity, marking a dramatic pivot into the neocloud market.

AI education company Classover has abandoned its original focus and rebranded as Kidz AI Inc., pivoting into the neocloud space with plans to build GPU-powered data centers. The company announced the shift on June 30, 2026, following a $100 million equity purchase agreement with Chardan Capital Markets signed in May.

Kidz AI has since raised $500.6 million in convertible secured financing, according to a company statement on May 29. The capital will be used to acquire Nvidia GPU clusters, including H100, H200, B300, and B200S models, and to deploy them in Tier 3+ data centers across the United States and globally.

...

Kidz AI formed a partnership with bare-metal GPU provider 1Legion to create a special purpose vehicle called Ousia Compute. Kidz AI owns the majority of the vehicle, which will invest $50 million in AI compute infrastructure. The joint venture will deploy Nvidia GPU clusters in Tier 3+ facilities across multiple U.S. locations and international sites.

Days later, Kidz AI announced a second partnership with Cyfuture.ai, an AI cloud and GPU infrastructure provider. This agreement gives Kidz AI access to Cyfuture.ai's full infrastructure stack, including GPU-as-a-Service, Inferencing-as-a-Service, and Tier III certified data center operations.

- $100M equity facility from Chardan Capital Markets for GPU and data center expansion.
- $500.6M in convertible secured financing raised on May 29, 2026.
- $50M joint venture Ousia Compute with 1Legion for GPU cluster deployments.
- Partnership with Cyfuture.ai for operational access to GPU and inference as a service.
- Nvidia H100, H200, B300, and B200S clusters planned for Tier 3+ data centers.

...

The pivot from education to AI cloud infrastructure mirrors a wider trend in the data center industry, where capital is flowing into specialized GPU clouds. Kidz AI CEO Stephanie Luo said the company is “positioning the company to become an important participant in the rapidly growing AI infrastructure sector.” The company will continue operating its AI education business alongside the new cloud division and is exploring robotics and industrial automation.
